title: extcap: Do not drain stderr on process exit
description:
Extcap child watch callback assumed that the stderr pipe is broken.
However the stdout and stderr pipes are not necessarily broken if the
child process spawned new processes that inherited standard handles.

Do not drain stderr in busy loop to prevent UI freeze. Stop capture
session only when all extcap watches are removed. Remove stdout and
stderr watches on capture stop timer (30 seconds) expiration, even if
the pipes are not broken.

Do not rely only on 0 bytes read to cease reading stdout and stderr.
Stop reading if the status is anything else than G_IO_STATUS_NORMAL
(especially it can be G_IO_STATUS_EOF).

notes.body: requested review from @stigbjorlykke

My current hypothesis regarding the issue is that reading past EOF on Mac OS hangs. If that hypothesis holds true, then it is possible that this commit alone won't fully solve the issue (albeit the race should be fairly small, but could easily be extended with specifically crafted extcap). The full solution would involve unrefing `stderr_io` and setting the pointer to NULL before returning `G_SOURCE_REMOVE` in `extcap_stderr_cb()`.

Considering https://stackoverflow.com/questions/20961797/reading-from-named-pipes-in-linux-vs-os-x the likelihood for the hypothesis is true is high. However if you get to test this commit before I rework it to handle the corner case, please let me know the result.

Unless I'm missing something, POSIX/the Single User Specification is...

...not as helpful as I'd like.

[The page for `read()`](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/read.html) says:

> When attempting to read from an empty pipe or FIFO:
> 
> * If no process has the pipe open for writing, read() shall return 0 to indicate end-of-file.
> * If some process has the pipe open for writing and O_NONBLOCK is set, read() shall return -1 and set errno to [EAGAIN].
> * If some process has the pipe open for writing and O_NONBLOCK is clear, read() shall block the calling thread until some data is written or the pipe is closed by all processes that had the pipe open for writing.

So a `read()` shouldn't block on an empty pipe where there is no writer, it should return EOF.

[The page for `select()`](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/select.html) says nothing about behavior specific to pipes, it just says it has to *work* on pipes, and that "If the *readfds* argument is not a null pointer, it points to an object of type **fd_set** that on input specifies the file descriptors to be checked for being ready to read, and on output indicates which file descriptors are ready to read."

So I would *guess* that an empty pipe with no process holding the pipe open for writing would be "ready to read", and thus that a `select()` should report that immediately rather than blocking.

A test program based on the program in the StackOverflow question, but with some more messages (and with a 1-second timeout in select to as not to completely spam my terminal ***AND FIXED SO THAT IT SETS `tv` BEFORE EACH `select()` CALL BECAUSE LINUX WILL UPDATE `tv`*** - which is allowed by POSIX/the SUS, just as not updating it is - ***AND TO DO AN `FD_ZERO()` BEFORE EACH `FD_SET()` SO THAT THERE AREN't OTHER FDS HANGING AROUND***) appears, once all three pipes are presumably closed on the write side (as all three `echo` commands writing to the three pipes have exited), to, in the `select()` calls on all three pipes:

* block, so that a timeout is reported, on macOS Big Sur;
* immediately return "ready to read" on Linux 5.15.0-43-generic in Ubuntu 22.04.

Given that, I'd say macOS is not following the SUS as I read it, which means either that 1) the SUS test suite doesn't test this particular case, so the problem wasn't caught and macOS was given the Official Seal Of Approval as a UNIX(R) or 2) I'm misreading something.

How does Mac OS handle the `read()` when `O_NONBLOCK` is not set? Does it return 0 only the first time when the pipe breaks (no process has the pipe open for writing)?

In other words, when `read(fd)` is called immediately after `read(fd)` returned 0, will the second `read()` return immediately or wait for something to connect to the other end of pipe?

changed this line in [version 2 of the diff](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/7706/diffs?diff_id=459447542&start_sha=64fb67d236f8ead0e41f1a7a7166db51f0213200#a460ce82517de094e48e578b825974f31852facf_1397_1476)

> In other words, when `read(fd)` is called immediately after `read(fd)` returned 0, will the second `read()` return immediately or wait for something to connect to the other end of pipe?

It returns 0 immediately (both on anonymous and named pipes, which I think are implemented by the same code path on most UN\*Xes, although there have been exceptions - as I remember, SunOS 3.2 and 4.x did so).

So this might be an issue with `select()` on macOS.  Time to dive into the kernel code (which, as I remember, involves the kqueue code).

On macOS, while `read()` behavior is fairly straightforward - whether in non-blocking mode or not, and whether reading from an anonymous pipe or named pipe, as soon as there are no writers left, you get an immediate EOF and keep getting immediate EOFs.

`select()` and `poll()`, however, are a different matter.

For anonymous pipes, as soon as there are no writers left, `select()` and `poll()` will return, indicating that the pipe is readable and, in the case of `poll()`, that it's been disconnected, with a subsequent `read()` getting an EOF, and that continues.

For *named* pipes, however, as soon as there are no writers left (i.e., a writer opens the pipe, writes to it, and then closes the pipe):

- with `select()`, the *first* `select()` call will return, indicating that the pipe is readable, and a subsequent `read()` will get an EOF, but a subsequent `select()` will block until somebody *else* opens the pipe and writes to it, later, rinse, repeat;
- with `poll()`, the `poll()` call just blocks, so the reader just hangs, with no indication that somebody closed the pipe on the other end.

I'll try this on the other BSDs, as well as on Linux and Solaris.  I suspect hilarity will ensue.

Linux (Ubuntu 22.04, 5.15.0-43-generic kernel), Solaris (11.4 CBE), FreeBSD (12.3-RELEASE-p5), OpenBSD (6.6): without `select()` or `poll()`, or with anonymous pipes, just like macOS.  With `select()` or `poll()` and a named pipe, what you might normally expect - after the last writer is gone, `select()` or `poll()` says you can read (with `poll()` noting the disconnect), and a subsequent `read()` gets an EOF, lather, rinse, repeat.

DragonFly BSD (5.8): a more consistent version of macOS, with both `select()` and `poll()` just blocking after the writer goes away, with no indication that somebody closed the pipe on the other end.

NetBSD (9.1): with anonymous pipes, just like everybody else.  With a named pipe, the *first* read after the writer goes away - and the `select()` or `poll()` before the first read - gives an immediate EOF with the `select()` and `poll()` returning immediately (with `poll()` *not* giving a disconnect indication), but a subsequent `select()`, `poll()`, or `read()` will block.  (At least there's a bit more consistency there.)

tl;dr: don't trust `select()` or `poll()` to do anything sensible on named pipes when the last writer closes the pipe.

BTW, according to my tests, reading past EOF on an *anonymous* pipe doesn't hang on *any* of the UN\*Xes on which I tested it; is the standard output or error of an extcap a *named* pipe in any circumstances?

Here's the test program, and two scripts that write out two strings 10 seconds apart, one of which writes to `/tmp/testfifo` and one of which writes to the standard output (the former exists because I was concerned that *somehow* redirecting the standard output to the test FIFO caused it to stay open after the process with the redirected standard output exited).

[piperead.c](/uploads/f45e96fe4cd100aad55b7571547144a1/piperead.c)

[writenamedpipe](/uploads/b08771dd3c36c607f531dee20d5e2c0e/writenamedpipe)

[writestdout](/uploads/3a1e6c0e217db56dee41c6adeb04ffc8/writestdout)

Thank you @guyharris for detailed analysis. The key note from your analysis is that the issue does not extend to use of GIOChannel for maxmind db reader. That is, the maxmind db reader will work fine.

The actual problem was that the extcap in question did spawn new process that kept the stdout/stderr alive even after the main extcap pid finished. The SIGTERM never made it to the grandchild, and the grandchild did not care about broken pcap pipe.

Another possibility for a hang while draining stderr is when extcap passes the stderr handle to subprocess it creates and the extcap exits (so Wireshark receives child watch callback and assumes that the handle is broken) but the subprocess continues. The hang currently would completely freeze the UI.

The situation could be remedied by removing the drain stderr loop and calling `capture_process_finished()` (and setting `extcap_pid` to `WS_INVALID_PID`) only when all watches are gone. Doing so would make the UI responsive (with the capture control actions disabled) regardless of how long it takes for pipes to break.

The 30 seconds timeout could be utilized for not only the process but also to stdout/stderr. That is, if there is extcap misbehaving in the way that it exits but leaves some other process with the stdout/stderr handles open, Wireshark would continue waiting on stdout/stderr only for up to 30 seconds.

To have the stdout/stderr outlive extcap pid, following (real-world) pattern can be used:
```
py3=`which python3`
$py3 $script_path/nrf_sniffer_ble.py "$@"
```

In my opinion, the pattern should be corrected to:
```
py3=`which python3`
exec $py3 $script_path/nrf_sniffer_ble.py "$@"
```

With `exec` the child will receive `SIGTERM` and thus will notice that Wireshark wants to close it (and if it does not care about `SIGTERM`, it will be forcefully killed after 30 seconds with `SIGKILL`). The extcap continued to live despite broken pcap pipe (dumpcap) so Wireshark has essentially no way of cleanly shutting it down without asking for trouble (trying to send SIGTERM to whole process tree).

The current solution is to cease reading stdout/stderr after 30 seconds. This results in the full wait (with responsive UI but in "stopping capture" state) when used together with the misbehaving extcap.

We didn't specify that the extcap process should make sure to terminate all child processes it creates when extcap exits. However, we didn't specify that Wireshark would do the cleanup (and Wireshark never did so). I believe the (implied) expectation is that the extcap should take care of processes it creates.

Note that in this case, the full 30 seconds case is inevitable when we will have graceful shutdown. The grandchildren won't notice SIGTERM and with graceful shutdown the extcap pipe won't be closed until the timeout expires. In other words, the grandchildren won't have any chance of knowing that Wireshark wants it to shut down. And Wireshark won't have any meaningful way of forcefully terminating the granchildren either.

I don't want to force Wireshark to keep track of the grandchildren as doing so in my opinion will lead to issues and for sure doing so will make more extcaps in the wild that do not handle it correctly (why bother if someone else will deal with it).
